items.title: Independent answer → AI answer → verification
items.school: Northeastern University, D'Amore-McKim
items.description: Students do the underlying work themselves, then use AI, compare the two, document discrepancies, and reflect on what the model got right or wrong.
items.what: Students iterate prompts, validate AI outputs against independent calculations, and submit the process documentation alongside a reflection. The workflow makes checking—not generating—the central assessed skill.
items.why: The assignment preserves foundational mastery while still teaching students to work with AI as a professional analytical partner.
items.adapt: Use this whenever a course contains a calculable, evidence-based, or model-based answer. Ask students to produce a human baseline first, then test an AI result against it and explain every material difference.

items.title: The three-step assignment: solve alone, use AI, evaluate AI
items.school: Lake Superior State University, Lukenda School of Business
items.description: One structure used across Management, Marketing, Accounting and Finance: students first analyse independently, then explore where AI could help, then prompt the tool and evaluate its output.
items.what: Step 1 protects the student’s own problem framing. Step 2 asks where AI has legitimate value in that discipline. Step 3 requires direct tool use, prompt writing, and critical evaluation of the result.
items.why: It changes AI from a shortcut into a decision-support tool and is deliberately designed to travel across disciplines without changing the learning objective.
items.adapt: A strong default template for any existing assignment you do not want to redesign from scratch. Keep the original assignment, add an explicit AI phase, and grade the comparison and judgement.

items.title: The five-step verification loop
items.school: University of South Florida, Muma College of Business
items.description: Define the question → build evidence with analytics tools → use AI to test hypotheses → verify against the data → produce an executive-ready recommendation.
items.what: AI is embedded inside the analytical workflow rather than added at the end. Students use it to test ideas and sharpen the narrative, but must verify outputs against their own evidence.
items.why: This is one of the few cases with measured learning outcomes: analytics competency stayed strong while AI-augmented analytics and responsible verification scores were higher.
items.adapt: Use the same loop for finance, marketing research, operations, strategy, or any course where students move from evidence to a recommendation.

items.title: Prompt it, then attack it
items.school: Florida State University
items.description: Students prompt ChatGPT, critique the response, and identify where the tool is useful, weak, or inappropriate while building their own case analysis.
items.what: The deliverable is not the generated answer. Students must identify advantages, disadvantages, limitations, and appropriate use cases in relation to a concrete strategic problem.
items.why: The model can generate content, but it cannot replace the student’s judgement about whether that content is fit for a specific managerial purpose.
items.adapt: Replace “use AI to answer” with “use AI to produce a position you must audit.” Grade the quality of the critique, not the fluency of the AI output.

items.title: Use AI on a real task, then reflect on where it helped and failed
items.school: St. John's University, Tobin College of Business
items.description: Students use AI in authentic disciplinary work and then make the reflection on usefulness and limitations part of the assessed output.
items.what: In the accounting-fraud example, students use AI to detect possible fraud in transaction data; in fintech, they interact directly with AI systems. In both, the student must judge the tool’s contribution rather than simply report a result.
items.why: The school frames the shift as moving learning from passive recall toward active critical reasoning.
items.adapt: Add a short “AI post-mortem” to any project: What did AI improve? What did it distort? What did you have to correct? What would you never delegate next time?

items.title: Group AI Use Log
items.school: Mount Royal University, Bissett School of Business
items.description: Teams document why they used AI, which tools they used, prompts, outputs, verification, and reflections as part of the submission.
items.what: The log sits beside a policy requiring students to verify factual claims, acknowledge AI use, and retain accountability. It turns disclosure from a vague statement into observable evidence of process.
items.why: The same artefact supports assessment and gives faculty visibility into how students actually work with AI.
items.adapt: Attach a one-page AI use log to group projects. Keep it structured and short enough that students can complete it honestly rather than treating it as compliance paperwork.

items.title: Assess a “substantial and substantive” share of verifiable human work
items.school: University of Oregon, Lundquist College of Business
items.description: Rather than trying to ban tools, the school requires a meaningful portion of assessment to rest on work that can be verified as the student’s own.
items.what: The rule protects genuine learning while allowing AI productivity gains elsewhere. It defines an assessment floor rather than a list of prohibited technologies.
items.why: It is tool-agnostic and therefore more durable than policies that name specific platforms.
items.adapt: For each course, identify which outcomes must remain visibly human: live defence, in-class analysis, oral reasoning, calculation, field evidence, or a decision trail. Build grading weight around those parts.

items.title: Ask for information before you are allowed to analyse
items.school: Western University, Ivey Business School
items.description: Students first decide what information they need and why. Only after making those requests do they receive the relevant information and proceed to analysis.
items.what: The learning event is upstream: framing the problem and deciding what evidence is necessary. Students later see what they failed to request, making omissions visible.
items.why: Ivey’s stated aim is to protect productive struggle and teach students how to question AI rather than simply use it.
items.adapt: For any case, release only a short brief first. Require students to submit their information requests and rationale before unlocking exhibits or data.

items.title: Students build valuation agents
items.school: University of Washington, Foster School of Business
items.description: Students build AI valuation agents so the deliverable is the analytical instrument itself—not merely a valuation result.
items.what: Foster’s discipline-specific approach asks finance and accounting students to build tools that embody valuation work. The school pairs this with an AI bootcamp for all incoming students.
items.why: Building the instrument exposes assumptions, data requirements, and the logic of professional judgement more clearly than asking AI for a final number.
items.adapt: Have students design a valuation copilot with explicit inputs, assumptions, checks, and escalation rules, then test it on two companies with different risk profiles.

items.title: Use AI to detect fraud, then audit the detector
items.school: St. John's University, Tobin College of Business
items.description: Students use AI to identify potential fraud in financial transaction data and then reflect on where the system was useful and where it was limited.
items.what: The important design choice is that the assignment does not stop at detection. Students must evaluate false confidence, missed patterns, and the evidentiary quality of the AI result.
items.why: Fraud detection is a natural setting for teaching that an anomaly flag is not the same thing as a professional conclusion.
items.adapt: Use a prepared transaction dataset with planted and ambiguous anomalies. Grade both detection quality and the student’s reasoning about what requires human investigation.

items.title: AI-powered risk simulation built by the lecturer
items.school: Florida State University
items.description: A faculty member built a risk simulation game on a no-code platform to teach human-capital risk management; students also beta-test it.
items.what: Students experience risk decisions inside a simulation and provide structured feedback that informs the next version of the tool.
items.why: It shows that “build” does not necessarily mean a large development project; a subject lecturer can create a narrow simulation around one difficult concept.
items.adapt: Choose one decision in your course that becomes clearer when students can see consequences unfold. Build a narrow branching simulation rather than a full platform.

items.title: AI for ideation and fact-checking — not for the maths
items.school: Florida State University
items.description: AI is explicitly allowed for ideation, fact-checking and copy editing in discussion boards, while computational work remains independent.
items.what: The permission is precise and tied to one assessment channel. Students can use AI as a secondary brainstorming tool without outsourcing the core quantitative skill the course is designed to develop.
items.why: A precise boundary is easier to teach and follow than a blanket ban or blanket permission.
items.adapt: Map each assignment into “AI can support” and “student must own” steps. Publish the boundary next to the assignment rather than in a generic policy page.

items.title: AI-supported case analysis and financial modelling
items.school: Iowa State University, Ivy College of Business
items.description: Accounting and finance classes integrate AI tools into case analysis and financial modelling as part of a broader discipline-specific curriculum.
items.what: The school positions AI alongside the field’s existing analytical tasks rather than as a separate technology topic.
items.why: This keeps the AI work close to the decisions finance students are expected to make professionally.
items.adapt: Give students a model they already build manually, then ask AI to stress-test assumptions, propose scenarios, or explain sensitivity—but require students to validate every numerical claim.

items.title: Portfolio management on top of a universal AI baseline
items.school: Georgia Southern University, Parker College of Business
items.description: Finance students use AI in portfolio-management work after completing mandatory AI literacy before their first class.
items.what: Because the baseline is handled upstream, the discipline course can focus on portfolio decisions rather than teaching prompting from zero.
items.why: It is a useful programme-design lesson: shared foundations free faculty to spend course time on domain judgement.
items.adapt: If your students already have baseline AI literacy, skip generic tool instruction. Start with a real portfolio decision and require explicit investment rationale plus model verification.

items.title: A course-specific AI Accounting Tutor
items.school: University College Dublin, College of Business
items.description: One of UCD’s funded faculty projects is a dedicated AI Accounting Tutor built as a subject-specific teaching tool.
items.what: The tutor is part of a portfolio of seven funded AI use cases across six subject areas. The college then shares the lessons through peer-led teaching sessions and its internal AI resource hub.
items.why: It shows a practical path from a small faculty experiment to a reusable subject resource without trying to build a school-wide platform first.
items.adapt: Start narrow: one course, one recurring student difficulty, and a tutor grounded only in approved course materials. Decide explicitly whether it should explain, ask questions, give hints, or check reasoning.

items.title: Marketing students rethink consumer privacy
items.school: University of Washington, Foster School of Business
items.description: Instead of focusing only on AI-generated content, marketing students examine how AI changes consumer privacy.
items.what: Foster assigns discipline-specific questions. In marketing, the emphasis is on what AI makes newly difficult for the field, not merely what it makes faster.
items.why: It moves AI integration from productivity to strategic and ethical judgement about the market itself.
items.adapt: Ask students to redesign a customer-data or personalization strategy under an explicit privacy constraint, then defend what data they would not collect even if technically available.

items.title: A dedicated AI session inside Marketing Research
items.school: SUNY Oswego, College of Business and Entrepreneurship
items.description: Generative AI is inserted as one focused session inside an existing course to explore how it can strengthen marketing research.
items.what: The integration is deliberately small: a single course session rather than a new course, making it a realistic entry point for faculty who are not ready for a full redesign.
items.why: It demonstrates that meaningful integration can begin with one well-bounded task in an existing syllabus.
items.adapt: Choose one research step—question design, desk research, qualitative coding, hypothesis generation—and redesign only that session around AI plus verification.

items.title: Customer Analytics + AI as the disciplinary frame
items.school: Northwestern University, Kellogg School of Management
items.description: AI is taught as part of customer analytics rather than as a generic capability, inside Kellogg’s broader data and analytics pathway.
items.what: The course title itself pairs the functional discipline and AI, reinforcing that the tool belongs inside customer analysis and decision-making.
items.why: This is exactly the “domain + AI” framing the report identifies as closer to how employers hire.
items.adapt: Structure a module around a customer decision—segmentation, churn, targeting, experimentation—and make AI one analytical layer rather than the topic of the module.

items.title: Assess students on explaining what the AI is actually solving
items.school: UC San Diego, Rady School of Management
items.description: Students are assessed on their ability to clearly articulate how generative AI is solving a business or technical problem.
items.what: The school combines “learn by doing” with explicit assessment of problem articulation, contribution to discussion, and application to a real challenge in a capstone.
items.why: Poor AI work often begins with a badly framed problem; grading the problem statement makes that invisible weakness visible.
items.adapt: Add a required “What problem is the AI solving?” section to any AI-enabled assignment, including what is out of scope and what success would look like.

items.title: AI inside a sales competition
items.school: Georgia Southern University, Parker College of Business
items.description: AI is incorporated into an assessment format students already take seriously: the sales competition.
items.what: Rather than inventing a new AI assessment, the school folds AI into preparation and analysis around an existing performance-based activity.
items.why: The format keeps AI tied to persuasive judgement, customer context, and human performance.
items.adapt: Use AI to prepare objections, persona hypotheses, or call plans, then assess the live human interaction separately from the AI-supported preparation.

items.title: GenAI analysis of the customer journey
items.school: Academic College of Tel Aviv-Yaffo (MTA)
items.description: The school uses discipline-specific GenAI applications including analysis of customer journeys.
items.what: AI is applied to a familiar marketing/CX artefact rather than taught as a standalone tool.
items.why: Customer journeys are rich in qualitative evidence and assumptions, making them a useful place to teach both pattern recognition and challenge of model-generated interpretations.
items.adapt: Give students real or synthetic interview data and ask AI to propose a journey map; then require students to challenge missing moments, false generalizations, and unsupported pain points.

items.title: Configure → Audit → Reframe → Defend
items.school: Suffolk University, Sawyer Business School
items.description: Students configure an organisation of AI agents to handle a business decision, audit what the system missed, reframe the problem, and defend the final decision.
items.what: Each scenario contains a hidden “Second Question”—a governance or fairness issue students only find if they refuse the framing handed to them. In one hiring scenario the mean reframe score was 28/100, and eight of nine teams failed to rebuild after the flaw was revealed.
items.why: The design makes strategic judgement and responsibility measurable instead of treating AI ethics as discussion-only content.
items.adapt: Take a familiar strategy case and deliberately hide a second-order issue: excluded stakeholders, biased data, an assumption embedded in the KPI, or a boundary the model never questions.

items.title: Faculty-built AI simulation labs across business disciplines
items.school: Carnegie Mellon University, Tepper School of Business
items.description: Tepper faculty have built 14 interactive AI-powered learning labs that simulate real business scenarios.
items.what: The labs sit inside a Collaborative AI Initiative focused on designing workflows that balance automated systems with human judgement and accountability.
items.why: A simulation lets students experience consequences and workflow design—skills that are difficult to assess on a conventional written assignment.
items.adapt: Do not start by building “an AI lab.” Start with one decision that has a consequence and at least one plausible wrong path. Build the simulation around that decision.

items.title: AI simulations, case preparation, and progressively harder tutoring
items.school: Western University, Ivey Business School
items.description: Ivey is redesigning case learning with simulations, AIBEL for case preparation, and Sidekick for progressive theory mastery.
items.what: The common principle is to preserve productive struggle while using AI to structure practice and questioning rather than simply give answers.
items.why: It treats structure—the order and difficulty of questions—as the educator’s value even when students have powerful generative tools.
items.adapt: Build a tutor that asks increasingly demanding questions and withholds the next layer until the student explains their reasoning, instead of a chatbot that answers immediately.

items.title: Student teams build agentic systems for real organisations
items.school: University of Miami, Miami Herbert Business School
items.course: Product Design in the Age of AI
items.description: Student teams create AI-powered agents, applications, analytics, and prototypes for real business partners.
items.what: The learning experience is deliberately AI-native and tied to consequential client problems rather than toy tasks.
items.why: Real clients force students to deal with requirements, constraints, handoff, and responsibility—not only the technical build.
items.adapt: Turn a capstone into a client brief where the deliverable is a functioning AI-enabled workflow plus a governance note explaining where humans remain in the loop.

items.title: Futureproof your career in the age of AI
items.school: Michigan State University, Broad College of Business
items.description: Students use AI tools to research how skill requirements are changing in their own field, then present their findings to peers.
items.what: The task makes AI personally relevant and requires students to investigate a moving labour-market question rather than consume a generic lecture on the future of work.
items.why: Students have a strong incentive to check the output because the conclusions affect their own career choices.
items.adapt: Ask each student to choose a target role and compare current job descriptions, emerging AI-related tasks, and human capabilities that remain essential; require source checking.

items.title: AI in real client consulting projects
items.school: Wake Forest University, School of Business
items.description: AI supports problem framing, hypothesis generation, and client preparation in real-world consulting projects.
items.what: The tool is used at specific stages of the consulting workflow rather than as a substitute for the final recommendation.
items.why: It exposes students to the professional skill of deciding where AI accelerates the work and where client context and human judgement dominate.
items.adapt: Mark AI-eligible moments in an existing consulting project: framing, hypothesis generation, interview guide drafting, synthesis, and red-team critique. Require the team to justify each use.

items.title: A political-savvy simulator
items.school: IESA, Instituto de Estudios Superiores de Administración
items.description: An AI agent plays a protagonist from a leadership case so students can practise organisational conflict and power dynamics in real time.
items.what: Students’ dialogue is used to develop and assess political astuteness and emotional intelligence, anchored in named leadership frameworks.
items.why: The simulation converts a static case into deliberate practice: students must act, adapt, and respond rather than only analyse what someone else should have done.
items.adapt: Choose one leadership case with a difficult stakeholder. Turn that stakeholder into a role-play agent with a clear agenda, constraints, and behavioural cues; debrief the student’s choices afterward.

items.title: LLMs for people analytics instruction
items.school: University College Dublin, College of Business
items.description: One of UCD’s funded faculty projects explores the use of large language models for teaching people analytics.
items.what: The project sits inside a portfolio of seven small AI teaching use cases funded across six subject areas, with peer dissemination afterward.
items.why: It is a practical model for faculty experimentation: narrow scope, subject-specific question, small funding, then internal sharing.
items.adapt: Use AI to analyse a controlled set of qualitative people data—engagement comments, interview notes, or competency evidence—then compare results with a human coding approach and discuss bias.

items.title: AI for personality analysis and team formation
items.school: Iowa State University / CENTRUM PUCP
items.description: Iowa State uses AI for personality analysis and team building; CENTRUM PUCP uses automated team formation based on Belbin Team Role Theory.
items.what: In these cases AI is not only teaching content—it shapes how student teams are formed or how interpersonal data is interpreted.
items.why: That makes the algorithm itself a teachable object: students can question what the system optimises and what it overlooks.
items.adapt: Let AI propose teams from a transparent set of criteria, then ask students to critique the composition and identify what the model cannot know about collaboration.

items.title: Hiring bias as the object of the assignment
items.school: Suffolk University / Florida State University
items.description: Students examine AI-supported hiring decisions where the important failure is accepting a shortlist without questioning how it was produced.
items.what: Suffolk’s scenario reveals an AI screener that filtered out almost all women before human review; Florida State uses AI in organisational staffing strategy evaluation.
items.why: The core HR lesson is not “AI is biased.” It is that managers are accountable for the decision pipeline, including what happened before the output reached them.
items.adapt: Give students a seemingly reasonable shortlist plus limited process information. Grade whether they ask for selection criteria, excluded candidates, and adverse-impact evidence before deciding.

items.title: Use AI to strengthen the capabilities that become more valuable because of AI
items.school: University of Miami, Miami Herbert Business School
items.description: The school explicitly develops and documents human capabilities such as communication, analysis, nurturance, execution, and strategy alongside AI.
items.what: The premise is that as AI becomes more capable, distinctively human skills become more—not less—important and should be intentionally assessed.
items.why: It prevents AI integration from crowding out the interpersonal and judgement capabilities business education is supposed to build.
items.adapt: For an AI-enabled assignment, add a second rubric dimension for the human capability the tool cannot provide: stakeholder empathy, negotiation, judgement, persuasion, or accountability.

items.title: Supply Chain AI Consulting with real employers
items.school: Purdue University, Mitch Daniels School of Business
items.course: MGMT 46900 Supply Chain & Operations Analytics Consulting
items.description: Students use AI tools in real projects with Amazon, KPMG, and Rolls-Royce and can earn a Supply Chain AI Consultant credential.
items.what: The course ties AI, operations analytics, employer projects, and a discipline-specific credential together. Purdue is also developing agentic and autonomous-systems capability with industry partners.
items.why: It shows what “domain + AI” looks like when made legible to employers: not a generic AI badge, but a supply-chain AI capability.
items.adapt: If you already run a live company project, define one AI-enabled workstream and make the student team document the operational decision, evidence, AI contribution, and human sign-off.

items.title: Use AI to solve optimisation problems
items.school: University of Washington, Foster School of Business
items.description: Operations students work with AI on optimisation problems as part of Foster’s discipline-specific AI design.
items.what: The AI activity is tied to a task the profession already performs rather than a general AI exercise.
items.why: Optimisation creates a natural opportunity to teach the difference between proposing a solution and verifying feasibility, constraints, and objective functions.
items.adapt: Let AI propose or explain an optimisation approach, but require students to specify constraints, verify the solution, and show how the recommendation changes when one constraint moves.

items.title: AI negotiation practice inside logistics
items.school: Georgia Southern University, Parker College of Business
items.description: The logistics and supply-chain department uses AI specifically for negotiation practice.
items.what: The skill is taught where the profession uses it, rather than being separated into a generic management elective.
items.why: It is a reminder that useful AI integration often means moving a familiar skill into its actual functional context.
items.adapt: Create supplier, carrier, or procurement role-plays with AI counterparties. Debrief on concessions, information gathering, BATNA, and total-cost trade-offs.

items.title: Specify software and digitalise a supply chain with GenAI
items.school: University of East Anglia, Norwich Business School
items.description: Students learn to specify software, write code using generative AI, and digitalise supply chains.
items.what: The emphasis is not coding for its own sake but using AI-enabled development to redesign a business process.
items.why: It connects technical prototyping to the operational question of how a supply chain should work differently.
items.adapt: Ask students to pick one broken handoff in a supply chain, specify an AI-enabled solution, create a lightweight prototype or workflow, and justify controls and metrics.

items.title: Required analytics course rebuilt around verification
items.school: University of South Florida, Muma College of Business
items.description: AI is embedded into the full data-to-decision workflow, with verification as a required step.
items.what: Students define a business question, build evidence with analytics tools such as Tableau, use GenAI to test hypotheses and refine narratives, verify outputs against data, and produce executive-ready recommendations.
items.why: The course generated reusable prompt templates, lab modules, and rubrics and reported measured gains in AI-augmented analytics and responsible verification.
items.adapt: Use this as the template for any data-heavy course: AI may interpret and challenge, but the evidence base remains explicit and auditable.

items.title: Direct coding agents as an architect, not a typist
items.school: Santa Clara University, Leavey School of Business
items.description: Students learn to direct AI coding agents as architects, with the course treated as a distinct learning design rather than simple AI augmentation.
items.what: Leavey distinguishes ordinary AI augmentation of an existing course from new-course status, which is reserved for genuinely distinct learning outcomes.
items.why: The focus is orchestration and specification: students must define what should be built, structure the work, and evaluate the result.
items.adapt: For a nontechnical business course, you can borrow the same principle without teaching software engineering: have students specify and supervise a simple AI-built tool for a real process.

items.title: Teach orchestration rather than single-model prompting
items.school: University of Illinois, Gies College of Business
items.description: Students learn to design systems where multiple agents work together under human direction.
items.what: Gies centres its emerging work on AI orchestration, supported by an AgentLab and project-based learning. The human-in-the-loop remains explicit.
items.why: The capability is closer to how advanced AI systems are actually deployed in organisations: as workflows and systems, not isolated chat interactions.
items.adapt: Have students design a multi-step agent workflow on paper before building anything: inputs, agent roles, handoffs, checks, failure points, and where human approval is mandatory.

items.title: Hint-based AI tutor instead of answer-giving chatbot
items.school: MIT Sloan School of Management
items.description: MIT Sloan uses a course-grounded assistant alongside a tutor that gives hints on problem sets rather than direct answers.
items.what: The instructional distinction is intentional: the tutor supports the student’s reasoning process without removing the productive work of solving the problem.
items.why: A hinting system can scale support while preserving the learning objective that would disappear if the model simply solved the task.
items.adapt: If you build a course bot, write a refusal policy around “no final answers.” Design a hint ladder: concept reminder → guiding question → partial structure → worked analogue.

items.title: Personalised synthetic datasets for every student
items.school: St. John's University, Tobin College of Business
items.description: An AI-enabled tool generates personalised synthetic data for homework so each student works with a different dataset.
items.what: Students can complete the same analytical learning objective without sharing identical numbers or outputs.
items.why: It designs the copying problem out of the assignment rather than relying on policing or detection.
items.adapt: Generate equivalent but non-identical datasets, cases, or scenarios per student. Keep difficulty and learning outcomes constant while varying the surface data.

items.title: Personalised synthetic data for every student
items.school: St. John's University, Tobin College of Business
items.description: An econometrics tool generates personalised synthetic data for homework so each student works with a different dataset.
items.what: Students still perform the econometric work, but the input data is individualised. The design reduces the value of copying without relying on a prohibition or detection mechanism.
items.why: It tackles academic integrity through assignment architecture while preserving the quantitative skill being assessed.
items.adapt: Use a common analytical question but generate a different clean dataset, parameter set, or scenario for each student. Keep the learning objective identical and grade the reasoning and model interpretation.

items.title: Use AI to build econometrics coding skill — not to replace the analysis
items.school: University College Dublin, College of Business
items.description: A funded faculty project uses AI to strengthen students’ coding skills in econometrics.
items.what: The project is one of UCD’s seven subject-area AI use cases. The emphasis is on using AI as support for learning how to code rather than as a black-box solver.
items.why: This lets less technical students get unstuck while keeping interpretation, model choice, and validation with the student.
items.adapt: Allow AI for code explanation, debugging, and alternative syntax. Require students to annotate what changed, explain the econometric choice, and validate outputs independently.

items.title: Economics inside AI-powered business simulations
items.school: Carnegie Mellon University, Tepper School of Business
items.description: Economics is one of the five disciplines covered by Tepper’s faculty-built AI-powered interactive learning labs.
items.what: The labs simulate business scenarios and are designed around workflows that balance automated systems with human judgement and accountability.
items.why: Simulation is useful when the learning objective is not only to calculate an answer but to make a decision under changing conditions.
items.adapt: Choose one economic decision with a trade-off—pricing, market response, resource allocation, or policy impact—and let the simulation react to the student’s choices before the debrief.

items.title: AI + Entrepreneurship accelerator modelled on Y Combinator
items.school: UC Berkeley, Haas School of Business
items.description: A hands-on accelerator course lets students prototype and test ideas in the market faster before raising capital.
items.what: AI changes the pace of experimentation: students can move from concept to prototype and market feedback within the course window, alongside Haas’s existing lean-startup approach.
items.why: The value is not “using AI in startups” but compressing the build-test-learn cycle enough that students can gather real evidence earlier.
items.adapt: Set a weekly evidence target—prototype, user test, market signal—not a slide-deck target. Let AI reduce build cost but keep customer evidence as the grading anchor.

items.title: Build MVPs through AI-enabled “vibe coding”
items.school: University of Wisconsin–Madison, Wisconsin School of Business
items.description: Students build minimum viable products inside an AI-enabled business solutions lab.
items.what: The course sits after a required introductory AI course in a three-course experiential sequence, so students build on a shared baseline instead of learning AI and product development simultaneously.
items.why: The order matters: foundation first, then construction. This keeps the lab focused on solving business problems.
items.adapt: Give students a narrow operational or customer problem and require a working MVP plus user evidence. Grade usefulness and iteration more than code sophistication.

items.title: Thirty-day AI product sprint with a real budget
items.school: Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Lally School of Management
items.description: Cross-disciplinary teams receive a budget to design, build, and deploy production-ready AI products in 30 days.
items.what: The deliverable is a working product that can serve as portfolio evidence, not a concept presentation.
items.why: A real budget forces prioritisation and trade-offs, making resource allocation part of the learning experience.
items.adapt: Give teams a fixed micro-budget and a 3–4 week deadline. Require them to choose what not to build, document assumptions, and deploy something testable.

items.title: AI competition with working MVPs and real organisational problems
items.school: UMass Lowell, Manning School of Business
items.description: Student teams develop business plans and working MVPs, including tools for medical coding, operations, coaching, exercise form, and academic advising.
items.what: The competition creates a funnel for practical ideas, including solutions to problems inside the university itself.
items.why: It gives students a visible reason to build while helping the school discover potentially reusable tools and operational improvements.
items.adapt: Run a challenge around 3–5 real problems submitted by internal teams or partner companies. Require a demo, evidence of use, and a short risk assessment.

items.title: NAIT — Negotiations AI Tutor
items.school: Florida State University
items.description: A purpose-built AI tutor explains topics, helps students prepare for negotiation activities, and answers routine course questions.
items.what: The tutor supports both learning and course administration, giving students a low-friction place to prepare before live negotiation exercises.
items.why: It targets a specific discipline and specific moments in the course instead of trying to become a general “everything bot.”
items.adapt: Ground a tutor in your course materials and restrict it to three jobs: concept clarification, practice preparation, and administrative Q&A. Keep live negotiation itself human.

items.title: Redesign communication assessments with AI feedback
items.school: Stetson University, School of Business Administration
items.description: Stetson uses AI-enabled feedback, redesigned communication assessments, and tools that can simulate case protagonists.
items.what: AI becomes a practice partner that can provide repeated feedback before the student performs or submits the final human communication.
items.why: Communication skill improves through iteration; AI can increase the number of low-stakes practice cycles without turning the final performance into AI-generated text.
items.adapt: Use AI for rehearsal feedback on structure, clarity, objections, or tone. Make the graded deliverable a live, recorded, or defended human performance.

items.title: Use résumés and interviews as the practice ground
items.school: Iowa State / Nebraska–Lincoln / Narayana MBA
items.description: Students use AI for résumé optimisation, interview practice, profile improvement, and business communication.
items.what: These are personally consequential but academically lower-risk tasks where students have a strong incentive to scrutinise the output.
items.why: Because the content is about the student, generic or inaccurate AI suggestions are easier to notice and discuss.
items.adapt: Have students ask AI to critique a résumé or interview answer, then require them to accept, reject, or rewrite each major suggestion with a reason.

items.title: Make ethics a graded, falsifiable capability
items.school: Suffolk University, Sawyer Business School
items.description: Students are scored on whether they detect and reframe a hidden fairness or governance problem inside an AI-supported decision.
items.what: The exercise produces a measurable result rather than an ethics discussion everyone can “pass.” In the published hiring scenario, teams performed poorly even after seeing the flaw, revealing a real learning challenge.
items.why: It teaches that responsible AI requires active refusal of a system’s framing, not passive awareness of bias concepts.
items.adapt: Put an ethical issue inside the task mechanics rather than in a separate reflection question. The student should have to notice it to succeed.

items.title: Green / Yellow / Red AI use by course
items.school: DePaul University, Driehaus College of Business
items.description: Every course is designated Green (full AI use with disclosure), Yellow (limited), or Red (no AI use).
items.what: The framework reduces ambiguity and treats transparent disclosure as a professional competency. The same school tracks student progress through a badge system.
items.why: Students do not have to interpret a vague institution-wide statement for every assignment; expectations are visible at course level.
items.adapt: Adopt a simple status at course or assignment level and define what “limited” means. Put the rule next to the assessment, not only in the syllabus.

items.title: Explore legal and ethical implications inside existing law courses
items.school: Iowa State University, Ivy College of Business
items.description: Students examine AI’s legal and ethical implications in courses where those questions already naturally belong.
items.what: The school does not require a new standalone AI ethics course to address the topic; it integrates AI into existing legal and ethical reasoning.
items.why: Students encounter responsible AI in the disciplinary context where they must actually make or defend a decision.
items.adapt: Use a current business process—hiring, pricing, marketing personalization, monitoring—and ask students to analyse legal, ethical, and governance risks as part of the core case.

items.title: Question AI before mastering it
items.school: American University, Kogod School of Business
items.description: First-year students learn to question AI’s accuracy, ethics, and biases before focusing on capability; MBA students compare AI-driven analysis with traditional methods.
items.what: The sequence makes scepticism and evaluation a prerequisite to fluency rather than an afterthought.
items.why: It establishes a habit of comparison and verification early, reducing the chance that students equate fluent output with reliable analysis.
items.adapt: Before teaching advanced prompting, give students two competing analyses—AI and non-AI—and grade their ability to identify evidence, assumptions, and failure modes.

items.title: Redesign assessment rather than rely on AI detection
items.school: University of Oregon / USF / Suffolk
items.description: Several schools protect learning by requiring verifiable student work, built-in verification, and defended judgement instead of relying on surveillance.
items.what: Oregon sets a floor for verifiable work, USF makes AI verification part of the workflow, and Suffolk makes defence and accountability part of the assessment.
items.why: The common move is to redesign what gets graded so the human contribution is visible and necessary.
items.adapt: For any high-stakes assignment, add at least one component AI cannot plausibly fake on its own: live defence, personal field evidence, in-class reasoning, process log, or verified calculation.

items.title: Teach privacy and accountability through the AI-use process itself
items.school: Mount Royal University, Bissett School of Business
items.description: Students must verify claims, acknowledge AI use, maintain accountability, and keep structured group AI use logs.
items.what: The framework is built around human-centredness, transparency, equity, privacy, accountability, and continuous improvement.
items.why: Responsible use becomes observable behaviour rather than a policy students read once.
items.adapt: Add three non-negotiable questions to AI-enabled assignments: What data did you share? What claims did you verify? Who is accountable for the final decision?
